title: Abhishek Sharma's 113 Off 38 Balls Seals Series for India
excerpt: India chased 199 in 13.2 overs in Wellington, beating New Zealand by six wickets with a record 118-run powerplay to lead 3-0.
body:
• India 199/4 in 13.2 overs beat New Zealand 198/3 in 20 overs by six wickets at Sky Stadium, Wellington, on 27 October 2026.
  • Abhishek Sharma made 113 off 38 balls, with nine fours and 11 sixes; his century came off 35 balls and Daryl Mitchell made an unbeaten 89 for New Zealand.
  • Abhishek and Vaibhav Sooryavanshi scored 118 in the powerplay, a men's T20I record, and put on 133 for the first wicket.
  • India lead the five-match series 3-0 with two games to spare; the fourth T20I is in Auckland on Friday.

Abhishek Sharma scored 113 off 38 balls as India chased down 199 in 13.2 overs to beat New Zealand by six wickets in the third T20I in Wellington on Tuesday and take an unassailable 3-0 lead in the five-match series. His century came off 35 balls. Reuters reported that he threatened his own record, a 30-ball century against Afghanistan in Delhi last month, the fastest by a batter from a full-member nation.

New Zealand set 198, Mitchell unbeaten on 89

India won the toss and bowled. New Zealand finished on 198/3 from 20 overs, with Daryl Mitchell unbeaten on 89 from the number three position. The hosts reached 58/1 in the powerplay and 150 in 15.4 overs, and Bevon Jacobs added 32 off 19 balls in a 50-run partnership with Mitchell, according to the match report and summary at Cricket World. Tim Seifert, Finn Allen and Glenn Phillips were the three wickets to fall. On most nights, 198 would have controlled the game. It gave New Zealand less than seven overs of control.

A record powerplay ends the contest

Abhishek and 15-year-old Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, promoted to open, scored 118 without loss in the first six overs, at 19.66 runs per over. That is a record for a men's T20I powerplay, beating the 116 Romania made against Serbia in 2021. India brought up their team fifty in 2.2 overs and their hundred in five overs. Sooryavanshi was caught at long-on off Matthew Fisher for 45, ending a first-wicket stand of 133 in the eighth over.

Abhishek reached his fifty in 15 balls. Mitchell Santner dropped him at extra cover on 92, losing the ball in the Wellington wind, and Abhishek reached his hundred by driving Kyle Jamieson to the fine-leg fence, marking it with Erling Haaland's meditation celebration. Jamieson dismissed him soon after, Glenn Phillips holding the catch near deep midwicket. By then India were 178/2 in the tenth over and needed 21 from ten overs. Shreyas Iyer and Sanju Samson fell late, but India closed on 199/4 with 40 balls unused.

"That was the plan for us. Just get the momentum for the team and keep going," Abhishek, the player of the match, said. Santner was blunt about the other side of it: "Pretty tough to stop those guys when they're going. We've seen it before, seen it in the IPL and obviously witnessed it here tonight in New Zealand."

What the numbers mean

This was Abhishek's fourth T20I century. The chase was built on scoring rates that remove the middle overs from the game: a strike rate of 297.37 for the top scorer, a powerplay worth nearly 60% of the target, and a required rate that fell below two runs an over before the halfway point of the chase. New Zealand's problem was not their total. It was that their new-ball bowlers, including recalled quick Fisher and Jacob Duffy in the opening over, were hit for 26, then 17, then 21 in the first three overs and never recovered a length the openers had to respect.

What's next

The series is decided. The fourth match is in Auckland on Friday, with the fifth to follow, and both sides now play for different things: India can test bench options around a settled opening pair, while New Zealand need a bowling plan for Abhishek that survives the first three overs. On this evidence, that plan, not their batting, is the series problem they have left to solve.
